skills.name: Location of firms: production and market factors

note.text: Location is the choice of where an activity operates. Relevant factors include inputs, customers, labour skills, power, water, transport, land and communication. Their importance depends on the activity. A bulky or perishable input can favour proximity to supply; customer contact may favour access to buyers. Cheap land alone does not make a site viable if essential services fail. A firm can face conflicting factors, so a location explanation must connect the factor to costs, revenue or feasibility.

sections.heading: Your goal and connections
sections.text: By the end, you should be able to explain a location factor’s effect on an activity and calculate a stated transport-cost difference. Builds on: firm objectives, scale and specialised demand. Leads to: comparing complete sites and the benefits or costs of industrial clusters.

sections.heading: Follow the local case
sections.text: A fictional processor near Buea compares input transport with access to customers. An urban repair service may value nearby clients, while an activity dependent on a specific resource faces a different constraint. No actual route, site, wage, tariff or safety condition is asserted; the figures supplied are invented comparisons.

sections.heading: Reason and check
sections.text: Name the product and its production needs first. Calculate the relevant transport component with consistent units, then ask what is missing. A saving on inputs may be offset by a larger outward-delivery cost. Explain why the same factor can matter differently to different activities.

cards.idea: Distinguish these features before judging a business.
example: input access: proximity or connection to the resources an activity needs.
market access: the ability to reach customers effectively.
labour suitability: availability of the skills and workforce needed for the activity.
infrastructure reliability: dependability of essential services and connections.

cards.idea: Use the stated case evidence to identify the economic feature.
example: A bulky-input processor compares the cost of bringing materials to each site.
A repair service considers how easily clients can reach it.
The firm checks relevant technical skills rather than headcount alone.
A processor checks power and water continuity before accepting cheap land.

cards.idea: Explain a consequence instead of assuming every option has the same effect.
example: input access: Activities require different inputs, so their location priorities differ.
market access: Accessibility can affect both service demand and distribution costs.
labour suitability: The type and capability of labour matter as well as its number.
infrastructure reliability: A site can be cheap yet fail an essential operating requirement.

questions.prompt: A fictional processor compares input transport. Site A costs {ain} CFA francs per load for {loads} loads; Site B costs {bin} per load for the same loads. How much lower is this input-transport cost at A?

misconceptions.explain: That is the saving per load; multiply by the number of loads.
Additions do not give the cost difference between sites.

solution: B minus A = {answer} CFA francs; other location factors remain to be compared.
